stories.title: Hank Williams
stories.dek: Twenty-nine years and a songbook for the ages
stories.body:
Hank Williams was born in rural Alabama in 1923 and began playing guitar as a boy. As a teenager he formed a band, the Drifting Cowboys, and played local clubs. He learned music from a street singer in Georgiana, Alabama, a Black bluesman named Rufus Payne, known as Tee-Tot. Williams later said Tee-Tot taught him how to play and how to put feeling into a song.

By 1947 he had a recording contract, and in 1949 his version of "Lovesick Blues" became a hit that took him to the Grand Ole Opry. At the Ryman Auditorium his first appearance brought the crowd to its feet, and they called him back for encore after encore. Over the next few years he wrote and recorded a stream of songs that have never gone away, among them "Your Cheatin' Heart," "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry," "Hey, Good Lookin'" and "Jambalaya."

His songs were plain and direct. They used everyday words, and they spoke of loneliness, love and heartbreak with a sharp eye. He wrote them for the ordinary people in his audience. Pop singers soon discovered them too, and artists like Tony Bennett and Rosemary Clooney scored hits with his tunes, spreading his songwriting far beyond country.

His private life was troubled. He had chronic back pain and drank heavily, and he missed shows. In August 1952 the Opry fired him for his unreliability. He went back to his old radio show in Shreveport and kept performing.

On December 31, 1952, he set out by car for a New Year's Day show in Canton, Ohio. His driver found him unresponsive in the back seat in the early hours of January 1, 1953. He was 29. Within days the news was everywhere, and his funeral in Montgomery drew a huge crowd. "Your Cheatin' Heart" was released after his death and became one of his most famous songs.

Williams made music for only about six years. Yet nearly every country singer who followed him has acknowledged his influence, and artists from Bob Dylan to Norah Jones have recorded his songs. His son, Hank Williams Jr., and later his grandchildren carried on the family name in music.

For many fans he is the figure from whom modern country starts, a poet of the honky-tonk who did not live to see thirty.

stories.title: Folsom Prison
stories.dek: A country star, a prison yard and a career reborn
stories.body:
In 1953 a young airman named Johnny Cash was stationed in West Germany with the U.S. Air Force. One evening he watched a film called Inside the Walls of Folsom Prison. The movie stayed with him, and he wrote a song, "Folsom Prison Blues," imagining a prisoner who listens to a train and thinks of freedom. Cash would play it for years.

By the mid-1960s his career had slowed. He had struggled with drug use, and his record sales had dropped. But he had always had a connection to prisoners, and he had played for inmates since 1957. He persuaded Columbia Records to let him record a concert in a prison. His producer, Bob Johnston, backed the plan.

On January 13, 1968, Cash, June Carter, Carl Perkins and the Tennessee Three played two shows at Folsom State Prison in California. The recording captured the roars and whistles of the inmates. Cash opened with a simple introduction: "Hello, I'm Johnny Cash." Then he went straight into "Folsom Prison Blues." The inmates reacted with delight, especially to the song's famous dark line.

The album came out in May 1968 and surprised the label by selling in huge numbers. The single of the title song became a hit, and the success brought Cash back to the top. He married June Carter that same year, in March, and the pair went on to perform together for decades. In 1969 he made a second prison album at San Quentin, which included "A Boy Named Sue."

Cash became a spokesman for prisoners and spoke about prison reform before a Senate subcommittee in 1972. His influence extended to the musicians who heard him. In 1958 a young inmate at San Quentin named Merle Haggard saw Cash perform and was moved. Haggard later became a country star himself.

The prison albums showed a different side of Cash, a man who sang for people others ignored. His black clothes and deep voice became a trademark, and the Folsom concert is still remembered as a landmark of live recording.

stories.title: The Outlaws
stories.dek: Two Nashville rebels and the Texas sound
stories.body:
In the early 1970s Nashville ran like a factory. Record labels used a small group of trusted studio musicians, chose the songs, and sold a polished, string-laden sound known as the Nashville Sound. Singers who wanted to follow their own ideas often found the door closed. Two of them were Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings.

Nelson had written major hits for others, among them "Crazy" for Patsy Cline and "Hello Walls" for Faron Young. Yet as a performer he never quite fit in Nashville. After a fire destroyed his house and he felt boxed in, he moved to Texas. By 1972 he was living in Austin, where he found audiences who loved his songs and didn't care how he dressed. He grew his hair long and wore a bandanna.

Jennings had a different path. He had played bass for Buddy Holly and, as a young man, gave up his seat on the plane that crashed in February 1959. He has described a last exchange with Holly, though accounts vary on the exact words. By the early 1970s he was fighting with his label over control of his records. In 1973 he made Honky Tonk Heroes, using his own band and mostly songs by Billy Joe Shaver. It was rough, direct and a success.

Nelson's breakthrough was the 1975 album Red Headed Stranger. It told the story of a fugitive preacher in a spare, quiet setting, with little more than his guitar, a piano and some drums. Columbia executives worried it sounded like a demo. The album became a hit, and the single "Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain" reached the top of the country chart.

In 1976 RCA gathered Jennings, Nelson, Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser on one album, Wanted! The Outlaws. The word outlaw stuck, and critics and fans used it for the whole movement. The record was a big seller, and it showed that country could be rougher and more personal.

Nelson went on to record "On the Road Again" in 1980. The Outlaws had broken a rule, that Nashville's way was the only way. Many country artists after them have followed their lead.
